slides.title: Serverless Computing Explained
slides.body:
Serverless Computing
Subheading: No Server Management
Elastic compute instances still require choosing and managing a virtual machine; serverless computing removes that server entirely, letting code run without any provisioning or capacity planning by the user.
Covers Function as a Service (FaaS): code triggered by events
Also covers Backend as a Service: managed databases, auth, storage
Provider owns all server provisioning, patching and capacity
User supplies only code or configuration, never infrastructure
Analogy: A hotel's room service exists only when a guest calls for it, with no staff cost while no calls arrive — exactly as a serverless function's resources exist only during an active invocation, with nothing to manage when idle.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: a 'Serverless' umbrella splitting into two boxes, FaaS (compute) and BaaS (managed services), with a shared label 'no server to manage' beneath both.
slides.notes: Stress that serverless is broader than a single compute service: it is any model removing server management. Note that BaaS returns later as managed databases and auth. Exam angle: define serverless versus FaaS precisely.

slides.title: What No Server Management Means
slides.body:
No Server Management
Subheading: What Disappears
Removing server management shifts operational work a virtual-machine user would normally own entirely onto the provider.
Provider patches the operating system and runtime automatically
Capacity is allocated per invocation, not sized in advance
No idle infrastructure cost when the function is not running
Billing follows actual execution time, not continuous uptime
Visual Guidance: Sketch of the AWS Lambda console function page labelled 'no instance type, no OS to patch here'.
slides.notes: Point to the AWS Lambda console as the real location where this shows up — it has no instance-sizing field, unlike EC2. Contrast with the instance sizing decision from the previous session. Exam angle: list the operational tasks serverless removes.

slides.title: Event-Driven Execution Model
slides.body:
Event-Driven Execution
Subheading: Compute On Demand
A traditional server process runs continuously, waiting for requests even when idle; a serverless function stays absent until a triggering event occurs, then runs and stops.
No continuously running process consumes compute between events
Execution begins only when an event source fires a trigger
Resource use and cost track actual run time, not uptime
The function instance disappears again once execution ends
Visual Guidance: Timeline sketch: an always-on server as one flat continuous bar beside a serverless function shown as short isolated spikes at each event.
slides.notes: Contrast an always-on EC2 instance with a function appearing only on trigger. Point out the table: initialization adds overhead only on the first call. Exam angle: event-driven execution versus a request-response polling loop.

slides.title: FaaS: The Execution Unit
slides.body:
FaaS Execution Unit
Subheading: Function Vs Instance
Function as a Service (FaaS) makes a single function invocation the unit a platform schedules and bills, far finer-grained than an entire virtual machine.
Visual Guidance: Side-by-side diagram: one continuously running EC2 box beside several small function boxes flashing only on events.
slides.notes: Point out that this granularity difference drives cost: functions bill in milliseconds, instances bill in hours. Exam angle: why is FaaS billing finer-grained than instance billing.

slides.title: The Execution Model Overview
slides.body:
Execution Model Map
Subheading: Four Core Pieces
Beyond knowing a function runs on trigger, Lambda's execution model defines exactly how an invocation starts, runs and ends.
Each piece below is configured separately in the function console
Handler contract: the fixed signature every function must implement
Stateless execution: no data survives reliably between separate invocations
Concurrency: how many invocations run at the same time
Visual Guidance: Four labelled boxes in a row: Trigger/Event, Handler Contract, Stateless Execution, Concurrency, each with a one-word icon.
slides.notes: Set up the four pieces as one map before going into each. Ask: which of these four decides how many copies of the function can run together? Answer: concurrency.

slides.title: The Handler Contract Explained
slides.body:
The Handler Contract
Subheading: Event Context Response
The handler contract is the fixed shape every Lambda function code must follow so the platform knows how to call it and read its reply.
event: payload carrying the trigger's data, JSON-like structure
context: runtime metadata — request ID, time remaining, memory limit
Return value becomes the response Lambda sends back to the caller
Configured handler name must match the function and file exactly
Analogy: An office counter hands every visitor a fixed form to fill (event) plus a note of office rules (context), and the clerk's written reply (return value) is what the visitor receives back — exactly as Lambda passes event and context into the handler and takes its return value as the response.
Visual Guidance: Box diagram: event and context arrows entering a 'handler' box, one return-value arrow leaving it labelled response.
slides.notes: Walk through event, context and return value as the three parts of one fixed contract. Point out context is metadata about the run, not the input data. Exam hook: ask what context exposes versus event.

slides.title: Triggers, Events And Invocation Types
slides.body:
Triggers And Events
Subheading: Invocation Types Explained
A trigger decides which service calls the function, and the invocation type decides whether the caller waits for a result.
API Gateway requests typically invoke the function synchronously
Asynchronous invocation: event is queued, caller gets acknowledgement only
Event shape varies by trigger — each service defines its own schema
Polling-based triggers batch several records into a single event
Visual Guidance: Two arrows from a caller box: one labelled 'sync — waits', one labelled 'async — queued', both feeding the handler box.
slides.notes: Separate the trigger source from the invocation type since both vary independently. Mention API Gateway as a synchronous example and S3 upload as asynchronous. Interviewers often ask which invocation type a given trigger uses.

slides.title: Why Execution Stays Stateless
slides.body:
Stateless Execution
Subheading: No Persisted State
Because an execution environment can be torn down and rebuilt at any point, a function cannot depend on anything it remembered from an earlier call.
Local variables and temporary disk space are not guaranteed to persist
Each invocation may land in a fresh or a reused environment
Durable data belongs in an external database, cache or storage service
Idempotent handler logic protects against duplicate retried events
Visual Guidance: Two environment boxes side by side, each handling one invocation independently, with a crossed-out arrow between them labelled 'no shared memory'.
slides.notes: Explain statelessness as the price paid for elastic scaling, not a limitation by accident. Give the example of a counter variable resetting unexpectedly between calls. Exam hook: ask why Lambda functions should write session data externally.

slides.title: Concurrency Across Invocations
slides.body:
Concurrency Model
Subheading: Scaling Via Environments
Statelessness is what lets Lambda run many invocations in parallel, each in its own isolated execution environment.
A concurrency limit caps how many environments run at once
Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for one function
Remaining capacity is shared across other functions in one pool
Exceeding the limit throttles further invocations with an error
Visual Guidance: Three parallel environment boxes stacked, each processing one invocation, with a limit line capping a fourth attempted box as throttled.
slides.notes: Tie concurrency back to the isolated environments just described — more concurrent events simply means more environments spun up together. Mention throttling as the failure mode of exceeding limits. Common interview question: what happens when concurrency limit is exceeded.

slides.title: Cold Start And Warm Start Lifecycle
slides.body:
Execution Env Lifecycle
Subheading: Cold Vs Warm
A serverless platform does not keep every execution environment running forever; whether one must be built from scratch decides if an invocation is cold or warm.
Cold start: a new execution environment is built before code runs
Warm start: an existing environment is reused, no setup needed
Every cold start runs two internal phases: init, then invoke
Idle environments are reclaimed after a period of inactivity
Visual Guidance: Timeline: Cold path (box 'new environment' → init → invoke → response) above a Warm path (box 'reused environment' → invoke → response), same end point.
slides.notes: Frame this as the map before going into causes and phases individually. Point out that warm start skips a whole stage, not just runs faster. Exam hook: ask what decides cold vs warm for a given call.

slides.title: Why Cold Starts Happen
slides.body:
Causes Of Cold Start
Subheading: What Triggers Setup
A cold start, the delay from building a fresh execution environment, happens whenever no idle environment is available to reuse for the incoming request.
First-ever invocation: no environment exists yet to reuse
Scale-out: extra concurrent requests need fresh environments
Idle reclaim: an unused environment was torn down earlier
New deployment: updated code forces a fresh environment build
Analogy: A shop restocks and opens its shutters only when the first customer of the day arrives, not before — just as the platform builds an environment only when a request actually needs one.
Visual Guidance: Four small icons (first call, traffic spike, idle clock, new deploy) each pointing into one 'new environment built' box.
slides.notes: Walk through the four causes as the reasons no warm environment was sitting ready. Everyday phrasing: nothing was 'kept on' for this request, so it had to be switched on. Exam hook: a deployment update is a cold-start trigger even under steady traffic.

slides.title: Init Phase And Invoke Phase
slides.body:
Init Vs Invoke
Subheading: Two Internal Phases
A cold start is not one delay but two stages stacked together: setting the environment up, then running the function logic inside it.
Environment freezes after invoke completes, ready for reuse
Warm invocations skip init entirely and start at invoke
Init overhead delays the handler before it even starts running
Visual Guidance: Horizontal bar split into two blocks labelled Init and Invoke, with a dashed line marking where a warm call would start.
slides.notes: Point at the table while explaining that init is setup work, invoke is the actual code. Mention that the console reports the two separately, so they must not be confused. Exam hook: ask which phase a warm call skips.
tables: Download code, start the runtime, run code outside the handler
Runs the handler with the event payload

slides.title: Reducing Cold Start Latency
slides.body:
Reducing Cold Starts
Subheading: Mitigation Strategies
Because init overhead adds latency before any code runs, several practices reduce how often it occurs or how costly it is.
Provisioned concurrency: environments pre-initialized, billed even when idle
Smaller deployment package: less code to download at init
Fewer, lighter dependencies: runtime starts up faster
Scheduled warm-up calls: prevent idle environments being reclaimed
Faster-starting runtimes: interpreted languages init quicker than JVM-based ones
Visual Guidance: Five small labelled boxes in a row, each under a 'lowers init time' arrow pointing to a shrinking latency bar.
slides.notes: Explain that provisioned concurrency trades idle cost for predictable latency, unlike pure pay-per-invocation. Everyday phrasing: keeping a few shops pre-opened costs rent even with no customer. Exam hook: ask why provisioned concurrency is not free despite serverless billing being usage-based.

slides.title: Serverless Limits Overview
slides.body:
Limits Overview
Subheading: Four Operational Boundaries
Every Function as a Service (FaaS) platform bounds how long, how much memory, how much data, and how much local disk a function may use, since unmetered execution would inflate cost indefinitely.
Execution timeout: maximum wall-clock time one invocation may run
Memory allocation: RAM assigned, with CPU scaled proportionally
Payload size: maximum request and response body size
Ephemeral storage: temporary local disk cleared after execution
Visual Guidance: Four-box diagram: Timeout, Memory, Payload, Ephemeral Storage, each with a limit icon.
slides.notes: Introduce the four limit categories before detailing each; mention the Lambda console's Configuration tab as where these are set. Interview hook: ask why serverless needs hard limits despite auto-scaling.

slides.title: Execution Timeout Explained
slides.body:
Execution Timeout
Subheading: Maximum Run Duration
A function that never finished would hold resources and billing open forever, so every invocation carries a maximum duration after which the platform forcibly stops it.
AWS Lambda timeout: configurable up to 15 minutes maximum
Default timeout is 3 seconds unless explicitly raised
Timed-out invocation returns a task timed out error
Long batch or streaming jobs need a different compute model
Analogy: A parking meter cuts off paid time regardless of whether the car owner is done — just as a function is terminated at its timeout regardless of whether the code has finished.
Visual Guidance: Timeline bar showing invocation start, running, and a red cutoff line at timeout.
slides.notes: Explain timeout caps cost and resource hold time, not just failures. Point to the General configuration section, the same place s10-serverless-demo's timeout is set in the lab. Exam hook: ask what happens to in-progress work at timeout — it is killed, not paused.

slides.title: Memory, CPU And Payload Limits
slides.body:
Memory & Payload
Subheading: Sizing And Data Caps
Memory is sized separately from the instance families studied earlier, because a function's memory setting also fixes its CPU share and its cost rate.
Higher memory raises per-millisecond cost, so right-sizing memory balances speed against spend, the same trade-off used when sizing compute instances.
Visual Guidance: Render the four-row table; highlight a small bar beside Memory showing CPU rising with it.
slides.notes: Stress that payload limits differ for synchronous versus event-driven calls, and memory also sets CPU power. Point to the memory slider used when configuring s10-serverless-demo. Exam hook: ask why the asynchronous payload cap is far smaller than the synchronous one.
tables: CPU scales up with memory, to several vCPUs
Container images allow up to 10 GB

slides.title: Ephemeral Storage Explained
slides.body:
Ephemeral Storage
Subheading: Temporary Local Disk
A function sometimes needs scratch space mid-execution — unzipping a file or caching a lookup — so each execution environment gets a temporary disk at /tmp, wiped when that environment is removed.
Default ephemeral storage is 512 MB per execution environment
Configurable up to 10,240 MB (10 GB) if needed
Data in /tmp does not persist across cold starts
Not durable: use managed databases or object storage instead
Analogy: A hotel room is cleaned out after checkout, leaving nothing for the next guest — just as an execution environment's /tmp storage is erased once that environment is recycled.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: execution environment box with a /tmp folder inside, arrow showing it wiped on teardown.
slides.notes: Clarify ephemeral storage is scratch space tied to the environment's lifecycle, not a database substitute. Point to the ephemeral storage field under Configuration, the same console area used for the practical function. Exam hook: ask what happens to /tmp data between two cold invocations — it is gone.

slides.title: BaaS and Serverless Anti-Patterns
slides.body:
BaaS & Anti-Patterns
Subheading: Section Landscape
Serverless computing covers more than functions. Backend as a Service (BaaS) supplies ready-made backend pieces, while certain workload shapes fit serverless poorly.
Backend as a Service (BaaS): managed database, authentication and storage used directly
Anti-patterns: workload shapes where FaaS billing or limits cost more than they save
Three anti-pattern cases: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load
Visual Guidance: Simple map: left box 'BaaS' with three sub-icons (database, lock, disk); right box 'Anti-Patterns' with three labelled workload icons.
slides.notes: Set up the two halves of this takeaway before going into either. Mention that BaaS removes even the function-writing step that FaaS still needs. Exam angle: distinguishing BaaS from FaaS is a common interview question.

slides.title: What Backend as a Service Is
slides.body:
Backend As Service
Subheading: BaaS Defined
Backend as a Service (BaaS) is a managed backend component an application calls directly through an API, with no custom function code or server to run.
Provider manages scaling, patching and availability of that backend piece
Covers data storage, identity checks and file storage as ready services
Billed per request or per resource used, not per function invocation
Analogy: Room service in a hotel delivers food or laundry on request without the guest owning a kitchen or laundry staff — just as BaaS delivers a database, login check or file store on request without the application owning or running that backend.
Visual Guidance: Icon of a phone call going to hotel reception, mirrored by an API call icon going to a cloud database icon.
slides.notes: Contrast with FaaS: FaaS still runs an application's own code per trigger, BaaS has no custom code at all. Ask: is a managed database call BaaS or FaaS?

slides.title: BaaS Services in AWS
slides.body:
BaaS Components
Subheading: DB, Auth, Storage
Each BaaS category maps to a specific managed AWS service that an application calls instead of running its own database, login or file server.
The common thread: each is reached by a direct API call, with no function or server standing between the application and the service.
Visual Guidance: Three-row diagram: application icon with arrows to DynamoDB, Cognito and S3 icons, each arrow labelled 'direct API call'.
slides.notes: Point to the real AWS console names so the mapping is concrete, not generic. Mention Cognito issues tokens, DynamoDB holds data, S3 holds files. Exam angle: naming the AWS service behind each BaaS category.
tables: A file server the application would run

slides.title: Why Serverless Breaks Down
slides.body:
Serverless Anti-Patterns
Subheading: When It Fails
Function as a Service bills per invocation and resets state after each run. Some workloads do not fit that model, and using serverless there costs more or fails outright.
Anti-pattern: a workload shape where FaaS's model costs more than a dedicated server
Mismatch shows up in cost, correctness, or both, not only speed
Three recurring cases: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load
Analogy: A daily commuter paying per taxi ride spends more than someone owning a car for the same fixed route — just as a workload invoked constantly, or needing a long single run, is billed and bounded in a way a dedicated server is not.
Visual Guidance: Two icons side by side: a taxi meter ticking versus a parked owned car, labelled 'per-ride cost' and 'fixed cost'.
slides.notes: Frame anti-pattern as a cost-and-fit mismatch, not a technical failure of serverless itself. Tie the taxi analogy forward to the steady-load case coming next. Exam angle: listing workload types unsuited to serverless is a standard interview question.

slides.title: Three Serverless Anti-Patterns
slides.body:
Three Anti-Patterns
Subheading: Jobs, State, Load
Long-running jobs, heavy state and steady load each break a different assumption FaaS makes, and each has a better-fitting alternative.
Reserved compute beats per-invocation pricing once load stays near continuous, roughly past 40% utilisation.
Visual Guidance: Three-row table matching this slide's rows, with each row's right-hand column in a distinct colour to mark a separate alternative.
slides.notes: Link timeout and stateless execution to what the execution-model and limits slides already defined — this is where that limit stops fitting a workload. Mention the utilisation threshold as the cost trigger an interviewer may probe.
tables: Exceeds the function's execution timeout limit
Execution is stateless; in-memory data is lost between runs
A server holding state in memory or on disk
Per-invocation billing costs more than a reserved instance running continuously

slides.title: BaaS and Anti-Patterns Recap
slides.body:
Section Recap
Subheading: BaaS And Fit
Backend as a Service removes the function entirely for managed data, auth and storage needs, while the anti-pattern cases mark where running custom code on FaaS is the wrong fit.
Choose BaaS when the need is a direct database, auth or storage call
Choose FaaS for short, event-triggered custom logic within its limits
Choose servers or containers for long jobs, heavy state or steady load
Visual Guidance: Simple decision flow: three boxes labelled BaaS, FaaS, Server/Container, each with its matching use case written below it.
slides.notes: Close by tying every limit discussed back to a concrete choice a learner makes in practice. This decision map matches what a system-design interview question would ask for.

slides.title: Building and Testing the Function
slides.body:
Task Overview
Subheading: What Gets Built
This exercise builds one AWS Lambda function and invokes it three times to see when AWS prepares a fresh execution environment and when it reuses one. It applies the execution model, cold-start and limits ideas to a live function. An AWS account with Lambda and basic IAM permissions is needed.
1. Create a Lambda function named s10-serverless-demo in one available region
2. Deploy the provided Python handler and confirm deployment succeeds
3. Create and save a test event, then invoke the function once
4. Record the first invocation's duration and initialization duration
5. Invoke the function two more times without any change
6. Record the third invocation's duration and check for initialization again
7. Compare both runs, then clean up the function, role and logs

slides.title: Function Created and Code Deployed
slides.body:
Create and Deploy
Subheading: Function and Handler
Lambda console showing s10-serverless-demo created successfully
This is the Lambda console right after s10-serverless-demo is created, confirmed by the green success banner. The diagram view shows no trigger or destination attached, matching a function invoked only through a manual test event.
Code editor showing the lambda_function.py handler file
This is the code editor showing lambda_function.py with the handler's function signature and a placeholder return statement. The deployed version replaces this placeholder with the handler that builds the JSON response and measures execution_time_seconds.

slides.title: Creating and Running the Test Event
slides.body:
Invoke the Function
Subheading: Test Event Run
Test event configuration panel for s10-test-event
This is the Test tab's event panel while creating a new test event. Synchronous invocation is selected, the event name is set to s10-test-event, and sharing is kept private before saving and running the test.
Successful test response with statusCode 200 and execution details
This is the Test tab after a successful run, showing statusCode 200 and a JSON body with the handler's message and execution_time_seconds. The Summary beside it lists function version, duration and billing details for that run.

slides.title: Comparing First and Later Invocations
slides.body:
Cold vs Warm
Subheading: Observed Summaries
First invocation summary showing Duration and Init duration
This is the first invocation's summary, showing Duration of 1.96 ms alongside an Init duration of 99.72 ms. The Init duration line is the evidence that AWS built a new execution environment before the handler ran.
Later invocation summary with no Init duration line present
This is a later invocation's summary showing Duration of 40.98 ms with no Init duration line present. The absence of that line is the evidence used to call this run a warm start, reusing the earlier environment.

slides.title: Expected Result and Wrap-Up
slides.body:
Expected Result
Subheading: What To Check
The finished exercise shows a deployed function responding with statusCode 200, a first invocation carrying a measurable Init duration, and a later invocation with no Init duration line. The full walkthrough is demonstrated in the recording, and a step-by-step practical guide follows the session video.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
1. Serverless Basics: No server management; event-driven execution; Function as a Service (FaaS)
2. The Execution Model: Triggers & events; the handler contract; stateless execution; concurrency
3. Cold Starts & Warm Starts: Causes of cold start; init phase vs invoke phase; mitigation strategies
4. Limits & Constraints: Execution timeout, memory, payload size & ephemeral storage
5. BaaS & Anti-Patterns: Backend as a Service: managed databases, auth & storage; when not to use serverless: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load
